summary: The note surveys how Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) are being piloted in schools after September 1, 2023, citing examples from San Diego, Lansing, and Austin. It covers benefits across science, literature, and art, alongside challenges such as cost, accessibility, the digital divide, technology dependency, and the need for teacher retraining. Educators and academics are quoted on engagement, equity, ethics, and the shift from delivering content to enabling discovery.
one_line: VR and AR are entering classrooms through pilot programs that boost engagement but raise cost, equity, ethical, and teacher-training challenges.
key_facts: Virtual Reality is a computer-generated simulation of a three-dimensional environment, while Augmented Reality superimposes computer-generated images on the user's view of the real world.

Professor Emily Tanner of the University of Tech Innovations said on October 15, 2023 that engagement is markedly higher when students are 'experiencing' rather than just 'learning', comparing it to walking through the Roman Colosseum's arches.
On November 5, 2023, Bright Tomorrow Charter School in San Diego announced a VR pilot program funded by tech grants and private donors.
In the Bright Tomorrow pilot, students dissected virtual frogs, circumnavigated the globe for geography lessons, and stepped into historical events.
Principal Mark Harrison of Bright Tomorrow said on November 20, 2023 that VR unlocked a curiosity he had not seen in his twenty years of teaching.
Accessibility and cost remain significant hurdles to integrating VR and AR, and schools often must partner with tech developers and educational consultants.
In the Lansing School District, Michigan, local software companies have helped develop custom VR modules aligned with district objectives since September 22, 2023.
Superintendent Dr. Lisa Sun said the Lansing district is ensuring every child, regardless of background, has an equitable chance to benefit from the new learning environments.
In science, students can conduct chemical experiments virtually, reducing risks and costs associated with physical labs.
Art teacher Juan Torres said at an ArteTech conference on December 2, 2023 that his students create and walk through their own 3D art installations.
Dr. Vanessa Reid, in a January 8, 2024 lecture on 'Ethics in Education', asked whether we are prepared for technology dependency and the psychological effects of immersive learning.
Joshua Klein, in a teacher training initiative in Austin, Texas, said on February 3, 2024 that teachers are shifting from delivering content to enabling discovery.
Concerns about the digital divide and overreliance on technology could exacerbate educational inequalities.
